strengths: Novel framing: applies conformal prediction to modular two-stage pipelines and proposes decomposing residuals into upstream (ΔR1) and downstream (R2) components, enabling stage-wise uncertainty attribution rather than treating pipelines as monolithic black boxes.

Reasonably thorough theoretical development: coverage guarantee for the additive-quantile construction (Theorem 1), an FWER-based procedure with formal high-probability risk control (Theorem 2), and an adaptive extension that inherits the long-run coverage guarantee of ACI-style methods.

Extensive experimental suite: synthetic upstream/downstream/covariate shift scenarios, two real-world datasets (automobile supply-chain/used-vehicle pricing and stock prices), and numerous ablations (τ, δ, γ, η, window length k), plus visualizations showing that the scaling parameters (a,b) and residual components respond interpretably to the type/location of shift.

Practical diagnostic value: the ability to identify whether upstream or downstream stages drive miscoverage could genuinely help practitioners target retraining efforts rather than retraining an entire pipeline, and the paper demonstrates this qualitatively (e.g., retraining only μ̂1 after an upstream shock).

Extensive appendix with proofs, additional heuristics (signed residuals), extensions to auxiliary data, multi-stage pipelines, and φ-mixing dependent data, showing an attempt at generality beyond the core two-stage IID setting.
weaknesses: The core coverage guarantee (Theorem 1) is quite loose: to obtain 1-α coverage one must set c+d=α, effectively splitting the miscoverage budget across two conservative union-bound events; the b=a=1 special case (Corollary 1) only yields 1-2α coverage, meaning the guaranteed method is inherently much more conservative than standard split conformal prediction for the same nominal levels, which likely explains much of the observed 'improved' coverage in experiments (i.e., it may simply be trading efficiency for higher effective coverage rather than being Pareto-better).

The scaled-quantile construction (Definition 4), which is central to the interpretability story (a,b weights), has no direct distribution-free coverage guarantee; Proposition 2 only shows existence of ideal parameters via IVT, and practical validity is entirely deferred to the FWER procedure, which is acknowledged to be conservative and can produce empty Λval (abstention) -- a significant practical limitation that is only partially mitigated by the ad hoc tolerance parameter τ.

Empirical comparisons are not clearly apples-to-apples: the proposed method consistently produces wider intervals and sometimes abstains entirely (NA rows in Table 1), while baselines always produce an interval; higher coverage at the cost of substantially larger width and abstention makes it hard to assess whether the method offers a genuine efficiency-adjusted improvement over baselines rather than just operating at an effectively stricter risk level.

Many of the paper's extensions (multi-stage, auxiliary inputs, multiple upstream models, φ-mixing relaxation) are relegated to the appendix with limited experimental validation and acknowledged scalability issues (the candidate set Λ grows exponentially with pipeline depth), making the 'general framework' claim in the main text somewhat overstated relative to what is rigorously demonstrated.

The adaptive algorithm's principal theoretical guarantee (long-run coverage) is essentially inherited unchanged from Gibbs & Candes' ACI update rule; the novel components (SELECTLAMBDA updates to a_t, b_t, c_t, d_t) are heuristic, and their optimality or effect on efficiency is not analyzed theoretically, only empirically via ablations.

The method requires the intermediate variable x to be observed in training/conformal/calibration data (Section 2 assumption), which is a nontrivial requirement not satisfied in many real black-box pipelines (e.g., learned latent representations); this key limitation is stated but not deeply examined or stress-tested.

The attribution claim that 'at least one component must represent a majority of the error' is a fairly trivial consequence of the triangle inequality (if a+b≥R then max(a,b)≥R/2) and is presented with more fanfare than its mathematical content warrants.

Real-world evaluation is limited to two datasets with relatively modest and sometimes mixed improvements (e.g., stocks dataset shows only marginal width/coverage differences versus ACI), and the covariate-shift experiment (Section 7.2/Appendix D.3.7) explicitly shows the method provides little to no benefit over baselines when shifts are not stage-asymmetric, narrowing the claimed scope of applicability.

strengths: The core idea of decomposing the end-to-end residual into upstream (ΔR1) and downstream (R2) components for a two-stage pipeline is a reasonably novel and intuitive framing that is under-explored in the conformal prediction literature, which largely treats models as black boxes.

The FWER-based calibration procedure (Section 5) for selecting scaling parameters (a,b) is methodologically sound in spirit, leveraging established risk-control machinery (Bates et al., Angelopoulos et al.) and provides a principled, if conservative, way to combine component-wise quantiles with formal (though weak) guarantees.

The adaptive extension in Section 6 cleanly builds on the Gibbs & Candes ACI framework while adding stage-wise sensitivity parameters (c_t, d_t) that preserve the long-run coverage guarantee; the diagnostic visualizations (e.g., Figures 11-13 showing a, b, ΔR1, R2 tracking the source of shift) are a genuinely useful qualitative contribution for practitioners.

The appendix is extensive, including multi-stage extensions, auxiliary-data variants, ϕ-mixing relaxations, and numerous ablations (τ, δ, γ, η, k sweeps), suggesting the authors explored the design space fairly thoroughly.
weaknesses: The central coverage guarantee (Theorem 1) is a loose union bound (1-c-d), and the proof itself admits "the stated result is looser than necessary," undermining confidence that the theoretical contribution offers a meaningfully tight or novel guarantee beyond naive Bonferroni-style combination of two conformal sets.

There appears to be an inconsistency between the main-text statement of Proposition 1 (a trivial triangle-inequality upper bound, proven in two lines in the main text) and the appendix's "Proof of Proposition 1," which instead proves the existence of ideal scaling parameters (a*, b*) — content that matches Proposition 2, not Proposition 1. This mislabeling/duplication raises concerns about the care taken in proof presentation and overall rigor.

The method requires the intermediate representation x to be fully observable on the conformal/calibration data (Section 2, assumption), which is a strong requirement that excludes many realistic modular pipelines (e.g., deep hidden representations, latent embeddings) and substantially narrows the claimed applicability to "modern machine learning systems" and "medical diagnosis" settings mentioned in the introduction.

Theorem 2's guarantee is a doubly-probabilistic (PAC-style) statement with an extra tolerance parameter τ and failure probability δ that must be tuned; in practice the paper shows this conservatism causes frequent abstention (NA results in Table 1 and Figure 14), which weakens the practical value of the "robust coverage" claim since the method sometimes simply refuses to produce an interval rather than deliver a usable one.

Empirical validation is limited in scale and statistical rigor: real-world datasets are small (monthly macro data spanning roughly a decade, ~1 year of daily stock data), baseline comparisons rely on single aggregate width/coverage numbers without significance testing or confidence intervals on the real-data results, and the covariate-shift experiment (Section D.3.7) shows the proposed method offers no real advantage over baselines, undercutting the generality of the claimed benefits.

The gains reported for the non-adaptive method come with substantially wider intervals (e.g., Table 1 shows ~25-50% wider intervals for modest coverage gains), and there is no principled efficiency-coverage tradeoff metric (e.g., interval score, CRPS) used to establish that the method is a genuine improvement rather than a trivial consequence of being more conservative.

The adaptive algorithm's core coverage guarantee is essentially inherited unchanged from Gibbs & Candes (2021) ACI, with the additional stage-wise parameters shown only to not interfere with the existing proof; this is an incremental theoretical extension rather than a new guarantee tailored to the decomposition.

No code or data release is mentioned, and critical implementation details (e.g., exact FWER algorithm used, candidate grid Λ construction, VAR/ARIMA ensemble specifics) are scattered across a very long appendix, making faithful reproduction difficult.

strengths: The core idea of decomposing end-to-end residuals into upstream/downstream components for modular sequential pipelines is a genuinely useful perspective that existing black-box conformal methods do not offer, and the paper develops it into a coherent framework rather than just a conceptual suggestion.

The theoretical development is reasonably complete for a paper of this scope: a triangle-inequality based residual decomposition (Prop. 1), coverage guarantees for the separate-quantile construction (Theorem 1), an existence result for ideal scaling parameters (Prop. 2), and a formal FWER-based risk-control guarantee for the practical scaled-quantile method (Theorem 2), plus an adaptive extension with an asymptotic long-run coverage guarantee inherited from Gibbs and Candes.

Extensive appendix material broadens applicability and demonstrates the authors considered many practical extensions: auxiliary covariates, multi-stage and multiple-upstream-model generalizations, relaxation to stationary phi-mixing sequences, and a careful discussion of why summed quantiles are not simple upper bounds on full-residual quantiles.

The experimental suite is unusually thorough: synthetic gradual and rapid upstream and downstream shifts, a controlled multi-phase shock simulation, two real-world datasets (automobile supply chain and used-vehicle pricing, and stock prices), comparisons against multiple strong adaptive baselines (ACI, PID, OCID, DtACI), and systematic hyperparameter ablations (tau, delta, gamma, eta, window length) that help build confidence the method behaves as claimed.

The stage-wise diagnostic capability (identifying whether upstream or downstream drives error, visualized via scaling parameter trajectories and residual ratio plots) is a meaningful practical contribution beyond interval construction, potentially guiding targeted retraining decisions.
weaknesses: The proof of Theorem 1 is difficult to follow and arguably informal: the implication chain from interval violation to events A1 and A2 is asserted rather than rigorously derived, and the exchangeability argument for the first-stage delta term presumes the two models are fixed and that the test point's inclusion does not alter the argument; because the downstream model is evaluated on both the true intermediate value and the predicted one for the same label, the two events being unioned are correlated, and this correlation is not carefully analyzed beyond a loose union bound.

The main practical construction, scaled component quantiles, has no finite-sample coverage guarantee on its own; the paper falls back on an existence-only result and then resorts to an FWER-based grid search over the scaling pair, which can be computationally expensive and, by the authors' own admission in the appendix, scales poorly (combinatorially) for multi-stage extensions, limiting applicability beyond the two-stage case emphasized throughout the main text.

The empirical gains over strong baselines such as ACI, PID, and OCID are often modest and come bundled with wider intervals or outright abstention, so the improved-coverage claims partly reduce to the proposed method being more conservative; no comparison is shown against these baselines run with an inflated nominal miscoverage level to control for this conservatism confound.

Real-world validation rests on only two single time series (one macro series and one small set of stocks) without repeated trials across multiple assets or datasets, limiting statistical confidence in the significance of the reported advantages, since coverage and width comparisons are based on a single realization of history rather than multiple independent real-world instances.

The core methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, combining known building blocks (split conformal prediction, FWER-based risk control in the style of Bates et al. and Angelopoulos et al., and Gibbs and Candes style adaptive conformal inference) with a triangle-inequality based decomposition; the theoretical contribution, while correct in spirit, is not particularly deep.

The method requires access to the true intermediate representation at calibration time across all three data splits, which may not always be available in practice, and this assumption is stated but not deeply interrogated or stress-tested.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation (many hyperparameters such as the scaling and quantile pairs, target level, FWER level, tolerance, step sizes, and window length), and some key practical details, such as the construction and granularity of the candidate grid and its computational cost, are deferred to the appendix without a clear upfront cost analysis in the main paper.

strengths: Novel framing: decomposing prediction residuals into upstream/downstream components provides a genuinely useful diagnostic capability (error attribution) that black-box conformal methods lack, addressing a practically relevant gap for modular pipelines (e.g., macro forecasting, medical imaging).

Reasonably rigorous theoretical development: coverage guarantees for the separate-quantile construction (Thm 5.2), existence of ideal scaling parameters (Prop 5.5), and a risk-controlled FWER-based selection procedure with finite-sample guarantees (Thm 6.1), plus an extension to stationary φ-mixing sequences for non-IID settings (Appendix C.2).

Long-run coverage guarantee is preserved in the adaptive extension by building on the well-established ACI update rule, and the adaptive λ-selection mechanism is intuitively tied to which residual component currently dominates the error.

Extensive empirical validation across synthetic (upstream/downstream/gradual/rapid/covariate shifts), and two real-world datasets (automobile supply chain and stock prices), with comparisons against a wide array of strong baselines (SC, WSC, ACI, PID, OCID, DtACI, ECI, and the closely related CC method).

Thorough and honest ablation studies (τ, δ, γ, η, k) and a single-stage baseline check confirming that gains stem from exploiting pipeline structure rather than merely improved point prediction, which strengthens the causal claim behind the method's benefits.
Practical guidance is provided (hyperparameter flowchart, default grid suggestions), improving usability and reproducibility, and code availability is mentioned.
weaknesses: The core theoretical guarantees are loose or non-constructive: Theorem 5.2/Corollary 5.4 give conservative union-bound-type coverage (c+d, 2α), and Proposition 5.5 only proves existence of ideal (a*,b*) via the intermediate value theorem without a practical way to find them, motivating the FWER procedure which is itself conservative by design and can abstain (Λval = ∅), meaning the method sometimes produces no interval at all — a nontrivial practical limitation not fully reconciled with the coverage-guarantee framing.

Empirically, the proposed method's intervals are often noticeably wider than baselines (SC, WSC, ACI, PID, OCID) except when compared to the extremely over-covering CC baseline; the main real gains appear mainly under specific severe/structural asymmetric shifts, while under covariate shift (Section D.4.7/Appendix) the method shows no clear advantage over baselines, tempering the significance of the contribution.

The method introduces many additional hyperparameters (a,b,c,d,α,δ,τ,γ,η,k) relative to standard conformal baselines; despite the provided flowchart, this adds practical complexity and tuning burden that may limit adoption.

Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to the most closely related prior work (Gong et al., 2023, CC), differing primarily in the use of FWER-controlled selection and an adaptive extension rather than a fundamentally new decomposition concept.

The paper explicitly acknowledges that summed component quantiles do not generally upper-bound the full residual quantile (Appendix B.1), which undercuts the clean theoretical motivation of the triangle-inequality-based decomposition and is only justified empirically ('occurs rarely').

Extension to genuine multi-stage pipelines (beyond two stages) is only sketched in the appendix and acknowledged to face an exponential blow-up in the parameter search space Λ, with only heuristic mitigations proposed, limiting the practical scope of the stated 'two-stage for simplicity, easily extended' claim.

The main paper is very terse relative to the 37-page appendix that carries most of the technical substance, proofs, and experiments; this heavy reliance on appendix material somewhat hurts self-containedness and readability of the core submission.

Selection of (a,b) from Λval by picking the pair with coverage 'closest to nominal on S^conf' in the non-adaptive experiments is not fully justified theoretically and could be seen as an ad hoc post-hoc selection step that is not covered by the stated FWER guarantee.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and underexplored problem: conformal prediction for modular, multi-stage pipelines rather than treating the whole pipeline as a monolithic black box.

The residual decomposition (ΔR1, R2) is simple and interpretable, and the paper builds a reasonably complete theoretical scaffold around it: coverage for separate-quantile intervals (Thm 5.2), existence of ideal scaling weights (Prop 5.5), and FWER-based risk control for selecting scaling parameters with finite-sample guarantees (Thm 6.1).

Extensive empirical evaluation across synthetic shift regimes (IID, gradual/rapid, upstream/downstream/covariate) and two real-world datasets (automobile supply chain and stock prices), compared against a wide set of modern baselines (SC, WSC, ACI, DtACI, PID, OCID, ECI, CC).

Thorough appendix material: hyperparameter ablations (γ, η, δ, τ, k), practical selection guidelines/flowchart, extensions to φ-mixing non-exchangeable data, auxiliary inputs, multi-stage/multi-upstream pipelines, and a useful single-stage-baseline ablation that attempts to isolate whether gains come from decomposition versus better point prediction.
The adaptive extension retains a long-run coverage guarantee inherited from Gibbs & Candès (2021), and the paper is transparent about the width/abstention cost of its robustness.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contributions are incremental: the decomposition itself follows directly from the triangle inequality (explicitly acknowledged as 'looser than necessary' in the proof of Thm 5.2), and the FWER calibration machinery is largely a direct application of existing risk-control/learn-then-test theory (Bates et al. 2021; Angelopoulos et al. 2025) and ACI-style updates (Gibbs & Candès 2021) rather than a new guarantee; Prop 5.5 (existence of ideal a*, b*) is an IVT argument with no constructive value.

The main comparator CC (Gong et al., 2023) is shown to 'severely over-cover' and produce uniformly wide intervals across virtually every setting (Tables 3, 4, Figures 5-6), making it a weak strawman; relegating this comparison to the appendix while emphasizing coverage gains over SC/WSC/ACI/PID/OCID in the main text risks overstating the paper's advantage, since much of the coverage improvement appears attributable to conservativeness (wider intervals, abstention) rather than a sharper decomposition.

The method introduces a large number of interacting hyperparameters (a, b, c, d, α, δ, τ, γ, η, k, Λ grid), and the paper's own ablations show strong sensitivity to several of these (e.g., δ causing abstention, γ causing instability) — this raises reproducibility and practical-usability concerns despite the provided flowchart, since optimal settings appear data/shift-dependent and are not learned in a principled way.

Real-world evaluations (automobile indicators, stock prices) are each a single run/time series without repeated trials or statistical uncertainty quantification, relying mainly on qualitative visual comparison (Figures 3-4, 7-13); this weakens the evidential strength of the real-data claims relative to the synthetic experiments.

The 'stage-wise attribution' claims are heuristic (comparing magnitudes of ΔR1 vs R2) rather than a rigorous causal or statistical attribution procedure, and the auxiliary propositions in Appendix A.2 (A.3, A.4) only loosely justify when each term approximates R, with informal 'intuition' substituting for formal guarantees on attribution correctness.

Significance is somewhat narrow: gains are concentrated in asymmetric, stage-specific shifts; under covariate shift affecting the whole pipeline (Appendix D.4.7) the method offers no meaningful advantage over standard adaptive conformal baselines, and the single-stage baseline ablation (D.4.8) shows that baseline conformal methods fail similarly regardless of pipeline structure, somewhat undercutting the centrality of the two-stage framing to the claimed benefits.

The paper is extremely dense, with the bulk of technical and empirical content (37+ pages) relegated to appendices; this makes the core contribution harder to isolate and assess, and several central claims (e.g., default parameter choices, robustness guarantees under δ, τ) are only substantiated deep in the appendix rather than in the main text.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated reframing of conformal prediction for modular two-stage pipelines: rather than treating the end-to-end model as a black box, the paper decomposes the prediction residual into interpretable upstream (ΔR1) and downstream (R2) components via a simple triangle-inequality-based upper bound, enabling genuine diagnostic attribution of error to pipeline stages.

Reasonably comprehensive theoretical treatment: coverage guarantees for the separate-quantile construction (Thm 5.2), an existence result for ideal scaling parameters (Prop 5.5), a rigorous FWER-based risk-control procedure with finite-sample coverage guarantees (Thm 6.1) built on learn-then-test machinery, and a long-run coverage guarantee for the adaptive variant inheriting from Gibbs & Candès (2021)-style analysis.

Extensive empirical validation across synthetic shift settings (upstream/downstream, gradual/rapid), two real-world time series (automobile supply-chain/used-vehicle data, stock prices), and a large number of ablations (τ, δ, γ, η, k, choice of c/d, signed-residual heuristic) as well as comparisons against a wide set of modern baselines (SC, WSC, ACI, DtACI, PID, OCID, ECI, and the closely related CC method).

Thoughtful additional experiments that strengthen the causal story, e.g., single-stage baselines (VAR/ARIMA) showing that gains are not merely due to a better two-stage predictor but specifically from exploiting the stage-wise decomposition, and a covariate-shift experiment showing the method does not overcompensate width when shifts are not stage-specific.

Practical extensions (auxiliary data, multi-stage models, φ-mixing non-exchangeable data) and hyperparameter selection guidelines/flowcharts that aid practitioners, along with honest acknowledgment of trade-offs (wider intervals, abstention under severe shift) rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: The central methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: the decomposition is a direct triangle-inequality split, and the calibration machinery (FWER/learn-then-test, ACI-style adaptive updates) is largely borrowed from existing conformal risk-control literature; the main contribution is the application/combination to a two-stage structure rather than fundamentally new conformal machinery.

The theoretical guarantees for the practically used "scaled" interval (Definition 5.3, the main method used in experiments) are not direct — exact coverage for arbitrary (a,b) is shown to exist (Prop 5.5) but not characterized, so the actual deployed guarantee relies entirely on the empirical FWER procedure (Thm 6.1), which is conservative and can return empty Λ_val (abstention), somewhat weakening the practical strength of the headline theoretical results.

The number of free hyperparameters (a, b, c, d, τ, δ, γ, η, k) is large, and although guidelines/flowcharts are provided, tuning in practice is non-trivial and the sensitivity analyses (Tables 5–11) show performance can vary substantially with these choices, raising concerns about robustness/ease of adoption.

The multi-stage extension (Appendix C.4) explicitly acknowledges that the candidate parameter grid Λ grows exponentially with the number of stages, and the proposed mitigation (freezing all but top-u components) is heuristic and untested empirically, leaving the core two-stage framing as the only well-validated setting despite motivating examples (e.g., medical imaging pipelines) that are inherently multi-stage/deep.

Real-world evaluations are restricted to relatively simple two-stage pipelines (linear/ensemble upstream models, small supply-chain and stock datasets); no experiments on larger, more realistic modular pipelines (e.g., deep neural network cascades) are provided despite such settings being used to motivate the paper in the introduction.

Presentation is dense, with a large fraction of the technical content (most proofs, extensions, and nearly all ablations) relegated to a very long appendix (37 pages), making the main text somewhat incomplete on its own and placing a heavy burden on readers to verify claims.

The Impact Statement is entirely generic and does not meaningfully engage with potential risks (e.g., over-reliance on abstention signals for retraining decisions, or misuse of "diagnostic" claims in high-stakes domains like the medical imaging application mentioned in the introduction).
